rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while limiting the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The intermediate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to probe selectivity in the crowded four-peak cluster and the final pair. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving room for subsequent gradient shallowing if needed.

Test the low-temperature endpoint with the same gradient to map the opposite selectivity response. This will help distinguish whether temperature alone can relieve the central cluster before adjusting gradient slope.

Use a shallower gradient at the best temperature to test whether the remaining close pairs gain resolution or change selectivity. The current 7.23-minute last peak provides some room to spread the separation before incurring a time penalty.
Shorten the fully resolved gradient by one grid step to bring the last peak below 10 minutes. This tests whether the critical pair retains R ≥ 1.5, which would achieve the maximum CRF of 1.0.

Shift the fully resolving gradient upward by 0.05 organic while preserving its slope and temperature. This should advance the late peaks toward a sub-10-minute finish while largely retaining their resolution.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope from injection 6 to improve the sole critical pair from R = 1.40 toward full resolution. The 0.75-minute margin before the time penalty should accommodate this adjustment and may yield CRF 1.0.

Injection 7 already achieves the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark while seeking a faster fully resolved separation. Raise the starting organic fraction one step, with the resulting shallower slope potentially helping preserve critical-pair resolution.
Slightly flatten injection 8’s gradient to recover the critical pair’s resolution while retaining its earlier elution window. This targets CRF 1.0 with a shorter separation than injection 7.

Raise the starting organic fraction to advance elution while further flattening the gradient to protect the critical pair. Injection 9 remains a maximum-score fallback as we test for a faster fully resolved method.

Raise temperature by one grid step from the fastest fully resolved method to test for earlier elution without losing critical-pair resolution. Injection 10 remains the fallback if temperature-dependent selectivity reduces the score.

Probe one further temperature step to see whether the late pair separates after an elution-order crossover and whether the central pairs remain acceptable. Retain injection 10 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test a modest temperature increase on injection 7’s fully resolved gradient. Its steeper slope may improve the late-pair selectivity seen at 30 C, while the lower starting organic fraction may preserve separation in the central cluster.

Slightly steepen injection 11’s gradient to test whether the final pair gains resolution while maintaining the nearly resolved central pairs. This also targets an earlier finish than its 8.01-minute last peak, with injection 10 retained as the maximum-score fallback.

The 30 C refinements trade central-pair resolution against the final pair, so test a distinct temperature-selectivity regime with a shallower gradient than the initial scouting runs. The maximum CRF is already secured; this explores another route to a faster fully resolved separation.

Test whether the shallower gradient separates the close pairs observed in the 60 C scouting run, while moving away from the co-elution pattern at 50 C. Keep injection 10 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Further flatten the promising 60 C gradient to test whether the remaining critical pair separates after a slope-dependent elution-order crossover. The last peak is expected to remain near 10 minutes, while the central pairs should gain separation.

The critical pair reverses order between 20 and 26 minutes, so a slightly steeper gradient may separate it on the faster side of that crossover. Test 18 minutes while checking that the central pairs retain full resolution.

Use a slope of 0.045 organic fraction per minute, just above injection 18’s 0.04444, to lift the R = 1.49 pair while preserving the central pairs. The lower endpoint should still be reached after all peaks elute, enabling a finer slope adjustment on the permitted grid.

Raise the starting organic fraction to advance elution while slightly flattening the gradient to protect the central pairs. Test whether this balance preserves full resolution in a faster run, retaining injection 19 as the fastest maximum-score benchmark.

Flatten injection 20’s gradient one step to improve its sole unresolved central pair. Monitor the later pairs for the slope-dependent crossover, retaining injection 19 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Increase the slope only slightly from injection 19, from 0.045 to 0.04583 per minute, to test the faster edge of its fully resolved window. The central pairs have little margin, so retain injection 19 if either drops below R = 1.5.

Injection 22 marks the faster slope limit at a 0.10 starting fraction, so test a lower start with a steeper gradient to seek more resolution margin. This targets a more robust maximum-score method while retaining injection 19 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved run.

Test an intermediate starting fraction and slope between the near-resolved 30 C methods to balance the central and final critical pairs. Injection 19 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method; this seeks an alternative with greater resolution margin.

Use the final injection to slightly flatten injection 9’s fully resolving slope, seeking greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Injection 19 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method at 7.45 minutes.
